15: # Notion Property Types Reference
16: 
17: **Scope:** the property-type system that a Notion data source's schema is built from. This is the row-and-column knowledge layer that makes `mcp-notion` a workflow mode: to create a page, an agent must supply property values in the exact shape the data source's schema demands, and to query a data source it must know which filter conditions each type supports.
18: 
19: **API baseline:** Notion API version `2025-09-03` (the data-sources era). Property behavior is stable across recent versions; markdown round-trip tools pin `2026-03-11` but do not change the property model.
20: 
21: **Verification status (2026-08-21):** the type set, config shapes, and value shapes below were confirmed against the live Notion API reference — `property-object`, `property-schema-object`, and `page-property-values`. Points that could not be pinned to a single confirmed shape are marked `VERIFY` with the endpoint that would confirm them. Do not invent property types or filter operators; confirm a data source's real schema with `retrieve-a-data-source` before composing values.
22: 
23: ---
24: 
25: ## 1. OVERVIEW
26: 
27: A Notion data source (see `database-model.md`) has a `properties` object: a map of property name to a config whose `type` field is one of the types below. Each property type appears in **three different shapes**, and an agent that conflates them will send malformed requests:
28: 
29: | Shape | Where it appears | What it describes |
30: |---|---|---|
31: | **Schema config** | `properties[name]` on `create-a-data-source` / `retrieve-a-data-source` | How the column is defined (options, format, expression, relation target) |
32: | **Page value** | `properties[name]` on `create-a-page` / `update-page-properties` | The cell value for one row, conforming to the schema |
33: | **Filter / sort** | `filter` and `sorts` on `query-data-source` | Which conditions the type can be queried and ordered by |
34: 
35: Two facts govern everything else:
36: 
37: 1. **Some types are read-only / computed.** `formula`, `rollup`, `created_time`, `created_by`, `last_edited_time`, `last_edited_by`, `unique_id`, and `verification` cannot be set on page creation or update. Attempting to write them fails.
38: 2. **`title` is mandatory and singular.** Every data source has exactly one `title` property; it controls the page title and cannot be removed.
39: 
40: ---
41: 
42: ## 2. THE PROPERTY TYPE CATALOG
43: 
44: The confirmed set is **22 schema property types** (`property-object`), of which `place` is documented as not fully supported. Two additional value-level entries exist: `verification` (a read-only value type surfaced on wiki pages, not a schema-configurable column) and `button` (a UI-only property with no API representation). See §6 for those two.
45: 
46: | # | Type | What it is | Config? | Writable? |
47: |---|---|---|---|---|
48: | 1 | `title` | Page title; exactly one per data source | none | yes |
49: | 2 | `rich_text` | Free-form formatted text | none | yes |
50: | 3 | `number` | Numeric value with a display format | `format` | yes |
51: | 4 | `select` | Single choice from predefined options | `options[]` | yes |
52: | 5 | `multi_select` | Zero or more choices from options | `options[]` | yes |
53: | 6 | `status` | Progress state grouped into To-do / In progress / Complete | `options[]` + groups | yes |
54: | 7 | `date` | A date or date range, time optional | none | yes |
55: | 8 | `people` | References to Notion users | none | yes |
56: | 9 | `files` | File attachments / external file links | none | yes |
57: | 10 | `checkbox` | Boolean | none | yes |
58: | 11 | `url` | Web URL string | none | yes |
59: | 12 | `email` | Email-address string | none | yes |
60: | 13 | `phone_number` | Phone-number string | none | yes |
61: | 14 | `formula` | Computed value from an expression | `expression` | no (computed) |
62: | 15 | `relation` | Links to pages in another data source | `data_source_id` + type | yes |
63: | 16 | `rollup` | Aggregates a related property via a relation | relation + target + `function` | no (computed) |
64: | 17 | `created_time` | Creation timestamp | none | no (auto) |
65: | 18 | `created_by` | Creating user | none | no (auto) |
66: | 19 | `last_edited_time` | Last-edit timestamp | none | no (auto) |
67: | 20 | `last_edited_by` | Last-editing user | none | no (auto) |
68: | 21 | `unique_id` | Auto-incrementing ID, optional text prefix | none (UI-managed) | no (auto) |
69: | 22 | `place` | Geographic location | `VERIFY` | `VERIFY` (documented "not fully supported") |
70: 
71: ---
72: 
73: ## 3. NO-CONFIG WRITABLE TYPES
74: 
75: These types carry no schema configuration — the schema entry is just `{ "type": "<name>", "<name>": {} }`. What matters is the **page-value shape** used when creating or updating a page.
76: 
77: | Type | Page-value shape | Example |
78: |---|---|---|
79: | `title` | array of rich-text objects | `{"title": [{"text": {"content": "Q3 Report"}}]}` |
80: | `rich_text` | array of rich-text objects | `{"Notes": {"rich_text": [{"text": {"content": "Draft"}}]}}` |
81: | `date` | `{start, end?}` ISO-8601; `end` optional for ranges | `{"Due": {"date": {"start": "2026-08-21", "end": "2026-08-25"}}}` |
82: | `people` | array of user references by id | `{"Owner": {"people": [{"id": "<user-uuid>"}]}}` |
83: | `files` | array of file objects (external URL or uploaded id) | `{"Docs": {"files": [{"name": "spec.pdf", "external": {"url": "https://…"}}]}}` |
84: | `checkbox` | boolean | `{"Done": {"checkbox": true}}` |
85: | `url` | string | `{"Link": {"url": "https://example.com"}}` |
86: | `email` | string | `{"Contact": {"email": "user@example.com"}}` |
87: | `phone_number` | string | `{"Phone": {"phone_number": "+1-555-0100"}}` |
88: 
89: Notes:
90: - `title` and `rich_text` share the rich-text array model; the difference is that `title` is the one designated page-title column.
91: - `files`: an **internal** (Notion-hosted) file requires a prior file upload — `{"file_upload": {"id": "<upload-id>"}}` — which is one of the mode's direct-API gaps (see `api-gap-tools.md`). An **external** file only needs its URL.
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. CONFIGURED WRITABLE TYPES
96: 
97: These require a config object in the schema, and their page values reference that config.
98: 
99: ### `number` — display format
100: 
101: Schema config: `{"number": {"format": "<enum>"}}`. Format is one of `number`, `number_with_commas`, `percent`, or a currency format (`dollar`, `euro`, `pound`, `yen`, `ruble`, `rupee`, `won`, `yuan`, `real`, `lira`, and ~40 more). Page value: a bare number, e.g. `{"Price": {"number": 42}}`. Format is display-only and does not change the stored value.
102: 
103: ### `select` / `multi_select` — options
104: 
105: Schema config: `{"select": {"options": [{"name": "High", "color": "red"}]}}`. Colors: `default`, `gray`, `brown`, `orange`, `yellow`, `green`, `blue`, `purple`, `pink`, `red`.
106: 
107: Page values reference an option **by name** (Notion creates the option if it does not exist, when writing to a `select`/`multi_select`):
108: - `select`: `{"Priority": {"select": {"name": "High"}}}`
109: - `multi_select`: `{"Tags": {"multi_select": [{"name": "backend"}, {"name": "urgent"}]}}`
110: 
111: On read, the value also carries `id` and `color`.
112: 
113: ### `status` — options plus groups
114: 
115: Schema config adds a `group` to each option: `{"status": {"options": [{"name": "In progress", "color": "blue", "group": "In progress"}]}}`. The three groups are `To-do`, `In progress`, and `Complete`; they are always present and are reconfigured through the Notion UI, not typically via the API (`VERIFY` whether `update-a-data-source` accepts group edits, via the `property-schema-object` reference). Page value: `{"State": {"status": {"name": "In progress"}}}`.
116: 
117: ### `relation` — link to another data source
118: 
119: Schema config: `{"relation": {"data_source_id": "<uuid>", "type": "single_property"}}` (or `dual_property`). The target data source **must be shared with the integration** or reads/writes of the relation fail. Page value: an array of page references — `{"Projects": {"relation": [{"id": "<page-uuid>"}]}}`. Full single-vs-dual design guidance lives in `database-model.md §5`.
120: 
121: ---
122: 
123: ## 5. COMPUTED AND READ-ONLY TYPES
124: 
125: None of these can be set on `create-a-page` or `update-page-properties`. They are populated by Notion. On read they carry a typed value.
126: 
127: | Type | Config (schema) | Read value shape |
128: |---|---|---|
129: | `formula` | `{"expression": "<formula>"}` | `{"formula": {"type": "number"\|"string"\|"boolean"\|"date", "<type>": …}}` |
130: | `rollup` | relation + target property + `function` | `{"rollup": {"type": …, "function": "<fn>", "<type>": …}}` |
131: | `created_time` | none | ISO-8601 string |
132: | `created_by` | none | user object |
133: | `last_edited_time` | none | ISO-8601 string |
134: | `last_edited_by` | none | user object |
135: | `unique_id` | none (prefix set in UI) | `{"unique_id": {"number": 17, "prefix": "TASK"}}` |
136: | `verification` | not schema-configurable (wiki feature) | `{"verification": {"state": "verified"\|"unverified"\|"expired", "verified_by": <user>, "date": {…}}}` |
137: 
138: Notes:
139: - `formula` and `rollup` are configured in the schema but their **values** are always computed — you author the `expression` / aggregation, never the result. Function catalogs and expression syntax are in `database-model.md §6-7`.
140: - `rollup` read values can be **truncated** for large related sets; the non-truncated read of a single property is a direct-API gap (`GET /v1/pages/{page_id}/properties/{property_id}`, see `api-gap-tools.md`).
141: - `unique_id` is read from `property-object` but is not created through a normal schema write; the incrementing counter and optional prefix are managed by Notion.
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 6. EDGE AND UNSUPPORTED TYPES
146: 
147: Three entries need explicit handling so an agent does not treat them like ordinary columns:
148: 
149: - **`verification`** — a real page-property **value** type (confirmed on `page-property-values`), used by Notion **wiki** verification. It reports `state` (verified / unverified / expired), a `verified_by` user, and an optional `date` range. It is **read-only** and is **not** a schema-configurable column type — it does not appear in the `property-schema-object` create/update type set. Read it; never try to write it or add it to a schema.
150: - **`place`** — appears in the `property-object` schema type list but is documented as **not fully supported**. Treat its config and value shapes as `VERIFY` (confirm current support against the `property-object` reference before relying on it); do not depend on it in generated schemas.
151: - **`button`** — a Notion UI property that triggers actions. It has **no API representation**: it is not in `property-schema-object` (cannot be created via the API) and not in `page-property-values` (no readable value). If a workspace column is a button, the API simply will not expose it as a settable/gettable property. `VERIFY` only if a future API version adds it.
152: 
153: The task brief's candidate list included `verification` and `button`; the reconciliation above is the confirmed outcome — `verification` is value-only and read-only, `button` is not in the API, and `place` is the schema-only type the brief omitted.
154: 
155: ---
156: 
157: ## 7. FILTER AND SORT SUPPORT
158: 
159: `query-data-source` filters by property, and the available operators depend on the property type. Compound filters nest sub-conditions under `and` / `or` arrays. Sorts take `[{"property": "<name>", "direction": "ascending" | "descending"}]` (or `{"timestamp": "created_time"|"last_edited_time", "direction": …}`).
160: 
161: | Type(s) | Filter operators |
162: |---|---|
163: | `title`, `rich_text`, `url`, `email`, `phone_number` | `equals`, `does_not_equal`, `contains`, `does_not_contain`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` |
164: | `number`, `unique_id` | `equals`, `does_not_equal`, `greater_than`, `less_than`, `greater_than_or_equal_to`, `less_than_or_equal_to`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` |
165: | `select`, `status` | `equals`, `does_not_equal`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` |
166: | `multi_select` | `contains`, `does_not_contain`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` |
167: | `date`, `created_time`, `last_edited_time` | `equals`, `before`, `after`, `on_or_before`, `on_or_after`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty`, plus relative ranges (`past_week`, `past_month`, `past_year`, `this_week`, `next_week`, `next_month`, `next_year`) |
168: | `checkbox` | `equals`, `does_not_equal` |
169: | `people`, `created_by`, `last_edited_by` | `contains`, `does_not_contain`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` |
170: | `files` | `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` |
171: | `relation` | `contains`, `does_not_contain`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` |
172: | `formula` | filtered by the formula's return type — nest the matching `string`, `number`, `checkbox`, or `date` filter under `formula` |
173: | `rollup` | filter by the underlying value type, or use `any` / `every` / `none` for `show_original` rollups (`VERIFY` exact wrapper via `query-a-data-source`) |
174: 
175: Sort support: writable and timestamp types sort directly. `formula` and `rollup` sortability follows their computed return type; confirm against `query-a-data-source` for a specific schema.
176: 
177: ---
178: 
179: ## 8. READ-ONLY VS WRITABLE — QUICK RULE
180: 
181: When building a `create-a-page` or `update-page-properties` payload, include **only** writable types. Strip these eight before sending, or the request is rejected:
182: 
183: `formula`, `rollup`, `created_time`, `created_by`, `last_edited_time`, `last_edited_by`, `unique_id`, `verification`.
184: 
185: Everything else in §3-§4 is writable. When echoing a page you just read back into an update, filter the property map by type first — round-tripping a full read (which contains computed values) is the most common cause of write failures.
186: 
187: ---
188: 
189: ## 9. RELATED RESOURCES
190: 
191: - `database-model.md` — the database → data source → page hierarchy, relations (single/dual), rollup functions, and Formulas 2.0 syntax and function families.
192: - `mcp-tools.md` — the official Notion MCP tool catalog (`retrieve-a-data-source`, `create-a-data-source`, `query-data-source`, page CRUD) and Code Mode invocation.
193: - `api-gap-tools.md` — direct Notion API calls for capabilities the MCP does not cover, including file uploads and non-truncated page-property-item reads.
194: - Notion API reference: `property-object`, `property-schema-object`, `page-property-values`, `query-a-data-source` on `developers.notion.com`.

6:   - "notion property schema"

13: ---
14: 
15: # Notion Property Types Reference
16: 
17: **Scope:** the property-type system that a Notion data source's schema is built from. This is the row-and-column knowledge layer that makes `mcp-notion` a workflow mode: to create a page, an agent must supply property values in the exact shape the data source's schema demands, and to query a data source it must know which filter conditions each type supports.
18: 
19: **API baseline:** Notion API version `2025-09-03` (the data-sources era). Property behavior is stable across recent versions; markdown round-trip tools pin `2026-03-11` but do not change the property model.
20: 
21: **Verification status (2026-08-21):** the type set, config shapes, and value shapes below were confirmed against the live Notion API reference — `property-object`, `property-schema-object`, and `page-property-values`. Points that could not be pinned to a single confirmed shape are marked `VERIFY` with the endpoint that would confirm them. Do not invent property types or filter operators; confirm a data source's real schema with `retrieve-a-data-source` before composing values.
22: 
23: ---
24: 
25: ## 1. OVERVIEW
26: 
27: A Notion data source (see `database-model.md`) has a `properties` object: a map of property name to a config whose `type` field is one of the types below. Each property type appears in **three different shapes**, and an agent that conflates them will send malformed requests:
28: 
29: | Shape | Where it appears | What it describes |
30: |---|---|---|
31: | **Schema config** | `properties[name]` on `create-a-data-source` / `retrieve-a-data-source` | How the column is defined (options, format, expression, relation target) |
32: | **Page value** | `properties[name]` on `create-a-page` / `update-page-properties` | The cell value for one row, conforming to the schema |
33: | **Filter / sort** | `filter` and `sorts` on `query-data-source` | Which conditions the type can be queried and ordered by |
34: 
35: Two facts govern everything else:
36: 
37: 1. **Some types are read-only / computed.** `formula`, `rollup`, `created_time`, `created_by`, `last_edited_time`, `last_edited_by`, `unique_id`, and `verification` cannot be set on page creation or update. Attempting to write them fails.
38: 2. **`title` is mandatory and singular.** Every data source has exactly one `title` property; it controls the page title and cannot be removed.
39: 
40: ---
41: 
42: ## 2. THE PROPERTY TYPE CATALOG
43: 
44: The confirmed set is **22 schema property types** (`property-object`), of which `place` is documented as not fully supported. Two additional value-level entries exist: `verification` (a read-only value type surfaced on wiki pages, not a schema-configurable column) and `button` (a UI-only property with no API representation). See §6 for those two.
45: 
46: | # | Type | What it is | Config? | Writable? |
47: |---|---|---|---|---|
48: | 1 | `title` | Page title; exactly one per data source | none | yes |
49: | 2 | `rich_text` | Free-form formatted text | none | yes |
50: | 3 | `number` | Numeric value with a display format | `format` | yes |
51: | 4 | `select` | Single choice from predefined options | `options[]` | yes |
52: | 5 | `multi_select` | Zero or more choices from options | `options[]` | yes |
53: | 6 | `status` | Progress state grouped into To-do / In progress / Complete | `options[]` + groups | yes |
54: | 7 | `date` | A date or date range, time optional | none | yes |
55: | 8 | `people` | References to Notion users | none | yes |
56: | 9 | `files` | File attachments / external file links | none | yes |
57: | 10 | `checkbox` | Boolean | none | yes |
58: | 11 | `url` | Web URL string | none | yes |
59: | 12 | `email` | Email-address string | none | yes |
60: | 13 | `phone_number` | Phone-number string | none | yes |
61: | 14 | `formula` | Computed value from an expression | `expression` | no (computed) |
62: | 15 | `relation` | Links to pages in another data source | `data_source_id` + type | yes |
63: | 16 | `rollup` | Aggregates a related property via a relation | relation + target + `function` | no (computed) |
64: | 17 | `created_time` | Creation timestamp | none | no (auto) |
65: | 18 | `created_by` | Creating user | none | no (auto) |
66: | 19 | `last_edited_time` | Last-edit timestamp | none | no (auto) |
67: | 20 | `last_edited_by` | Last-editing user | none | no (auto) |
68: | 21 | `unique_id` | Auto-incrementing ID, optional text prefix | none (UI-managed) | no (auto) |
69: | 22 | `place` | Geographic location | `VERIFY` | `VERIFY` (documented "not fully supported") |
70: 
71: ---
72: 
73: ## 3. NO-CONFIG WRITABLE TYPES
74: 
75: These types carry no schema configuration — the schema entry is just `{ "type": "<name>", "<name>": {} }`. What matters is the **page-value shape** used when creating or updating a page.
76: 
77: | Type | Page-value shape | Example |
78: |---|---|---|
79: | `title` | array of rich-text objects | `{"title": [{"text": {"content": "Q3 Report"}}]}` |
80: | `rich_text` | array of rich-text objects | `{"Notes": {"rich_text": [{"text": {"content": "Draft"}}]}}` |
81: | `date` | `{start, end?}` ISO-8601; `end` optional for ranges | `{"Due": {"date": {"start": "2026-08-21", "end": "2026-08-25"}}}` |
82: | `people` | array of user references by id | `{"Owner": {"people": [{"id": "<user-uuid>"}]}}` |
83: | `files` | array of file objects (external URL or uploaded id) | `{"Docs": {"files": [{"name": "spec.pdf", "external": {"url": "https://…"}}]}}` |
84: | `checkbox` | boolean | `{"Done": {"checkbox": true}}` |
85: | `url` | string | `{"Link": {"url": "https://example.com"}}` |
86: | `email` | string | `{"Contact": {"email": "user@example.com"}}` |
87: | `phone_number` | string | `{"Phone": {"phone_number": "+1-555-0100"}}` |
88: 
89: Notes:
90: - `title` and `rich_text` share the rich-text array model; the difference is that `title` is the one designated page-title column.
91: - `files`: an **internal** (Notion-hosted) file requires a prior file upload — `{"file_upload": {"id": "<upload-id>"}}` — which is one of the mode's direct-API gaps (see `api-gap-tools.md`). An **external** file only needs its URL.
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. CONFIGURED WRITABLE TYPES
96: 
97: These require a config object in the schema, and their page values reference that config.
98: 
99: ### `number` — display format
100: 
101: Schema config: `{"number": {"format": "<enum>"}}`. Format is one of `number`, `number_with_commas`, `percent`, or a currency format (`dollar`, `euro`, `pound`, `yen`, `ruble`, `rupee`, `won`, `yuan`, `real`, `lira`, and ~40 more). Page value: a bare number, e.g. `{"Price": {"number": 42}}`. Format is display-only and does not change the stored value.
102: 
103: ### `select` / `multi_select` — options
104: 
105: Schema config: `{"select": {"options": [{"name": "High", "color": "red"}]}}`. Colors: `default`, `gray`, `brown`, `orange`, `yellow`, `green`, `blue`, `purple`, `pink`, `red`.
106: 
107: Page values reference an option **by name** (Notion creates the option if it does not exist, when writing to a `select`/`multi_select`):
108: - `select`: `{"Priority": {"select": {"name": "High"}}}`
109: - `multi_select`: `{"Tags": {"multi_select": [{"name": "backend"}, {"name": "urgent"}]}}`
110: 
111: On read, the value also carries `id` and `color`.
112: 
113: ### `status` — options plus groups
114: 
115: Schema config adds a `group` to each option: `{"status": {"options": [{"name": "In progress", "color": "blue", "group": "In progress"}]}}`. The three groups are `To-do`, `In progress`, and `Complete`; they are always present and are reconfigured through the Notion UI, not typically via the API (`VERIFY` whether `update-a-data-source` accepts group edits, via the `property-schema-object` reference). Page value: `{"State": {"status": {"name": "In progress"}}}`.
116: 
117: ### `relation` — link to another data source
118: 
119: Schema config: `{"relation": {"data_source_id": "<uuid>", "type": "single_property"}}` (or `dual_property`). The target data source **must be shared with the integration** or reads/writes of the relation fail. Page value: an array of page references — `{"Projects": {"relation": [{"id": "<page-uuid>"}]}}`. Full single-vs-dual design guidance lives in `database-model.md §5`.
120: 
121: ---
122: 
123: ## 5. COMPUTED AND READ-ONLY TYPES
124: 
125: None of these can be set on `create-a-page` or `update-page-properties`. They are populated by Notion. On read they carry a typed value.
126: 
127: | Type | Config (schema) | Read value shape |
128: |---|---|---|
129: | `formula` | `{"expression": "<formula>"}` | `{"formula": {"type": "number"\|"string"\|"boolean"\|"date", "<type>": …}}` |
130: | `rollup` | relation + target property + `function` | `{"rollup": {"type": …, "function": "<fn>", "<type>": …}}` |
131: | `created_time` | none | ISO-8601 string |
132: | `created_by` | none | user object |
133: | `last_edited_time` | none | ISO-8601 string |
134: | `last_edited_by` | none | user object |
135: | `unique_id` | none (prefix set in UI) | `{"unique_id": {"number": 17, "prefix": "TASK"}}` |
136: | `verification` | not schema-configurable (wiki feature) | `{"verification": {"state": "verified"\|"unverified"\|"expired", "verified_by": <user>, "date": {…}}}` |
137: 
138: Notes:
139: - `formula` and `rollup` are configured in the schema but their **values** are always computed — you author the `expression` / aggregation, never the result. Function catalogs and expression syntax are in `database-model.md §6-7`.
140: - `rollup` read values can be **truncated** for large related sets; the non-truncated read of a single property is a direct-API gap (`GET /v1/pages/{page_id}/properties/{property_id}`, see `api-gap-tools.md`).
141: - `unique_id` is read from `property-object` but is not created through a normal schema write; the incrementing counter and optional prefix are managed by Notion.
142: 
143: ---
144: 
145: ## 6. EDGE AND UNSUPPORTED TYPES
146: 
147: Three entries need explicit handling so an agent does not treat them like ordinary columns:
148: 
149: - **`verification`** — a real page-property **value** type (confirmed on `page-property-values`), used by Notion **wiki** verification. It reports `state` (verified / unverified / expired), a `verified_by` user, and an optional `date` range. It is **read-only** and is **not** a schema-configurable column type — it does not appear in the `property-schema-object` create/update type set. Read it; never try to write it or add it to a schema.
150: - **`place`** — appears in the `property-object` schema type list but is documented as **not fully supported**. Treat its config and value shapes as `VERIFY` (confirm current support against the `property-object` reference before relying on it); do not depend on it in generated schemas.
151: - **`button`** — a Notion UI property that triggers actions. It has **no API representation**: it is not in `property-schema-object` (cannot be created via the API) and not in `page-property-values` (no readable value). If a workspace column is a button, the API simply will not expose it as a settable/gettable property. `VERIFY` only if a future API version adds it.
152: 
153: The task brief's candidate list included `verification` and `button`; the reconciliation above is the confirmed outcome — `verification` is value-only and read-only, `button` is not in the API, and `place` is the schema-only type the brief omitted.
154: 
155: ---
156: 
157: ## 7. FILTER AND SORT SUPPORT
158:

Sorts take `[{"property": "<name>", "direction": "ascending" | "descending"}]` (or `{"timestamp": "created_time"|"last_edited_time", "direction": …}`).
160: 
161: | Type(s) | Filter operators |
162: |---|---|
163: | `title`, `rich_text`, `url`, `email`, `phone_number` | `equals`, `does_not_equal`, `contains`, `does_not_contain`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` |
164: | `number`, `unique_id` | `equals`, `does_not_equal`, `greater_than`, `less_than`, `greater_than_or_equal_to`, `less_than_or_equal_to`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` |
165: | `select`, `status` | `equals`, `does_not_equal`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` |
166: | `multi_select` | `contains`, `does_not_contain`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` |
167: | `date`, `created_time`, `last_edited_time` | `equals`, `before`, `after`, `on_or_before`, `on_or_after`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty`, plus relative ranges (`past_week`, `past_month`, `past_year`, `this_week`, `next_week`, `next_month`, `next_year`) |

169: | `people`, `created_by`, `last_edited_by` | `contains`, `does_not_contain`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` |

174:

176: 
177: ---
178: 
179: ## 8. READ-ONLY VS WRITABLE — QUICK RULE
180: 
181: When building a `create-a-page` or `update-page-properties` payload, include **only** writable types. Strip these eight before sending, or the request is rejected:
182: 
183: `formula`, `rollup`, `created_time`, `created_by`, `last_edited_time`, `last_edited_by`, `unique_id`, `verification`.

186:

188:

1: ---
2: title: README Template and Selection Guide
3: description: Concise guidance for project, skill, feature and component README files, with routing to the code-folder README template when developer topology is the main need.
4: trigger_phrases:
5:   - "readme selection guide"
6:   - "project readme template"
7:   - "skill readme routing"
8:   - "narrative readme structure"
9: importance_tier: normal
10: contextType: general
11: version: 1.2.1.0
12: ---
13: 
14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.
155: 
156: ---
157: 
158: ## 6. FILLABLE SCAFFOLD
159: 
160: Copy this scaffold, then remove sections that do not apply.
161: 
162: ````markdown
163: ---
164: title: "[PROJECT_OR_FEATURE_NAME]"
165: description: "[One-sentence description]"
166: trigger_phrases:
167:   - "[search phrase]"
168: version: 1.0.0.0
169: ---
170: 
171: # [PROJECT_OR_FEATURE_NAME]
172: 
173: > [One-sentence purpose statement.]
174: 
175: ---
176: 
177: ## 1. OVERVIEW
178: 
179: [Explain what this is, who it is for and why it exists.]
180: 
181: ### Key Statistics
182: 
183: | Metric | Value |
184: |---|---|
185: | Status | [Current state] |
186: | Version | [Version or release channel] |
187: | Main audience | [Who uses this] |
188: | Operating modes | [Mode count or short list] |
189: 
190: ### How This Compares
191: 
192: | Capability | This Project | Related Option |
193: |---|---|---|
194: | [Capability] | [Current behavior] | [Difference] |
195: 
196: 
197: ---
198: 
199: ## 2. QUICK START
200: 
201: ```bash
202: # Install or prepare
203: [command]
204: 
205: # Verify
206: [command]
207: ```
208: 
209: Expected result: [what success looks like].
210: 
211: 
212: ---
213: 
214: ## 3. FEATURES
215: 
216: ### Key Features
217: 
218: | Feature | What It Does |
219: |---|---|
220: | [Feature] | [Current behavior] |
221: 
222: 
223: ---
224: 
225: ## 4. REQUIREMENTS
226: 
227: | Requirement | Minimum | Notes |
228: |---|---|---|
229: | [Runtime or tool] | [Version] | [Why it is needed] |
230: 
231: 
232: ---
233: 
234: ## 5. STRUCTURE
235: 
236: ```text
237: [root]/
238: +-- [path]/        # [Purpose]
239: `-- [file]         # [Purpose]
240: ```
241: 
242: | Path | Purpose |
243: |---|---|
244: | `[path]` | [Role] |
245: 
246: <!-- For items needing more than one line, use the itemized pattern
247:      from Section 4 instead of this table. -->
248: 
249: 
250: ---
251: 
252: ## 6. CONFIGURATION
253: 
254: | Option | Default | Purpose |
255: |---|---|---|
256: | `[OPTION]` | `[value]` | [What it controls] |
257: 
258: 
259: ---
260: 
261: ## 7. USAGE EXAMPLES

12: ---
13: 
14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137: 
138: ---
139: 
140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143: 
144: ```yaml
145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:
149:   - "[search phrase]"
150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.
155: 
156: ---

159:

21: 
22: ## 1. OVERVIEW
23: 
24: ### Purpose
25: 
26: cupt provides a terminal interface to ClickUp designed for agent-driven workflows. Every read command supports `--json` for machine-readable output. Completion uses automatic per-list status resolution so agents never need to hardcode status names. The `--offline` flag uses a local cache populated by `cupt prefetch`, enabling operation without network access.
27: 
28: ### When to Use
29: 
30: - You need a daily ClickUp task operation from the terminal.

33: - You need to keep working without network access.
34:

36: - `cupt done` resolves the correct closed status per list automatically
37: - `--dry-run` on `cupt done` previews without writing
38: - `--offline` enables cached operation after `cupt prefetch`
39: - `--json` on all read commands gives structured output

8: # mcp-click-up Skill
9:

11:

13: 
14: ## 0. MARKDOWN FORMATTING CONTRACT — READ BEFORE ANY CLICKUP WRITE
15: 
16: ClickUp shows plain text literally. Markdown sent through a plain-text path shows up in the ClickUp UI as raw `### Heading`, `**bold**`, and `- [ ]` text. Whenever the content contains ANY markdown syntax, use the markdown-aware parameter for the operation. On the Code Mode manual (`clickup_official`), checked against the server's schema on 2026-10-08:
17: 
18: | Operation | Required parameter |
19: | --- | --- |
20: | Task create or update | `markdown_description` (the server has no plain `description` or `markdown_content` parameter) |
21: | Document page create, update or read | `content_format: "text/md"` |
22: | Task read-back | `include: ["description"]` on `clickup_get_task` |
23: 
24: On the raw ClickUp v2 REST API, `markdown_content` is also accepted on task update and `include_markdown_description=true` returns markdown, both live-verified 2026-07-15. The claude.ai ClickUp connector was not re-checked on 2026-10-08.
25: 
26: **Push shape for a markdown artifact:** the document's H1 becomes the task `name` (drop it from the body); strip internal HTML comments and processing metadata; everything else travels verbatim.
27: 
28: **Failure symptom:** literal `###` or `**` visible in a ClickUp task means someone used the plain `description` field. That is the defect, not a rendering bug.
29:

# Create a page (`notion_create-a-page`)

## 1. OVERVIEW

`notion_create-a-page` is one of the Notion MCP server's 7 Pages tools (`../../references/mcp-tools.md` §5 Pages). It creates a new page under a parent — either an existing page (`page_id`) or a data source (`data_source_id`), the schema-holding child of a database in Notion API 2.0.0 — optionally seeding it with `properties`, `children` blocks, an `icon`, and a `cover`.

The Code Mode callable form is `notion["notion_create-a-page"]` — bracket access, not dot access, because the tool name contains hyphens (`notion.notion_create-a-page` parses as subtraction and is invalid JavaScript). The official Notion MCP has no view tool. Views are Notion's saved table/board/list/calendar/timeline/gallery/form/chart/map/dashboard layouts over a database, each with its own filters and sorts. The REST API exposes a full CRUD-plus-query surface: 8 endpoints covering create, list, retrieve, update, delete, run-query, paginate-cached-results, and delete-cached-query.

1	Code Mode uses the local stdio server, because the remote OAuth server cannot complete its browser authorization step in a headless context. The local server is deprecated but still functional; treat that as a known risk to plan a migration around, not a wrong choice for headless automation.
     2	
     3	### Agent Safety Invariants
     4	
     5	Always share a page or database with the integration before operating on it. An unshared target returns HTTP 403, and a missing share is the single most common cause of "not found" confusion. Always respect the rate limit: about 3 requests per second per integration, with bursts allowed. On HTTP 429 (`rate_limited`) or 529 (`service_overload`), honor the `Retry-After` header and back off with jitter; centralize retries in the HTTP layer, not per tool. Always let the server pin the API version per operation, and never hardcode a single version across markdown and non-markdown tools. Treat tokens as opaque strings; do not validate them with a regex. Never auto-modify `opencode.json`, the Code Mode config lives in `.utcp_config.json`. Confirm every tool name with `tool_info()`; never guess it. An empty `search` result is valid and common, do not fabricate pages.

     4	
     5	Reach for this skill when you need to create, read, update or organize Notion pages, blocks, data sources, comments or users from an agent. Reach for the official MCP path for any CRUD operation in its six domains. Reach for the direct API path when the work is a file upload, a view operation, a non-truncated property read or an async-task poll. Reach for the knowledge-layer references before authoring any property, relation, rollup or formula write.
